prompt: In a Go codebase, why can grep for a method name like `.Save(` be insufficient to know which implementation actually runs at a given call site?
choices: Because Go allows method overloading across unrelated types
Because any type whose method set satisfies an interface can define a method with that same name, and grep can't tell which concrete type is wired in at runtime
Because grep ignores package boundaries when searching Go source
Because Go interfaces are erased from the source before compilation and can't be grepped

prompt: You build a Go binary with plain `go build -o app .`, then run `dlv exec ./app` and set a breakpoint inside a small helper function. Execution never stops there, even though you're certain the function runs. What's the most likely cause?
choices: Delve cannot attach to binaries built with `go build`, only with `dlv debug`
The compiler's default optimizations likely inlined the small function into its caller, leaving no separate instruction to break on
Go binaries never contain any debug symbols under any build
The breakpoint must be set using a fully package-qualified function name instead of a file:line

prompt: In `go tool pprof` output, a function showing high "flat" time should be read as:
choices: A function that is called very infrequently
A function whose own code, excluding the functions it calls, is consuming that much CPU time
A function located near the top of main.go
A function that only affects memory allocation, never CPU time

prompt: Given `result += e + "\n"` inside a loop over N strings in Go, what happens to running time as N grows, and why?
choices: It grows linearly with N, because Go string concatenation is O(1) per append
It grows roughly quadratically with N, because each `+=` allocates a new string and copies the entire prior result into it
It stays constant, because Go interns and reuses all string literals automatically
It panics once N exceeds roughly 10,000, because Go strings have a fixed maximum length

prompt: How does contributing to the core Go standard library (the `golang/go` repository) differ from contributing to most Go open-source projects hosted on GitHub?
choices: It works identically — fork the repo and open a normal GitHub pull request
It only accepts contributions mailed in as raw patch files, with no tooling support
Its GitHub mirror does not accept pull requests; real changes go through Gerrit code review via the `git-codereview` tool
It requires a paid cloud account before any change can be submitted

prompt: While stopped at a breakpoint inside `LedgerService.Deposit`, you run `print s.store` in Delve and see `main.Store(*main.MemStore) 0xc0000a4010`. What does this tell you that reading `service.go` alone never could?
choices: The exact numeric value of the `amount` argument
That the interface field `store` is, at this exact moment, actually holding a `*MemStore` rather than some other type that also satisfies `Store`
That the running program has a memory leak
The compiled byte size of the `Store` interface type

prompt: After reading a "good first issue" and understanding the bug, what's the most reliable next step before writing the fix itself?
choices: Open a PR immediately with your best guess at the correct fix
Write a test that reproduces the reported bug, confirm it fails, then make it pass
Rewrite the entire module you suspect is responsible, to be thorough
Wait for a maintainer to personally assign you the issue before touching any code

prompt: What does `git commit -s` add to a commit, and why do some open-source projects require it before merging a PR?
choices: A GPG signature that encrypts the diff contents
A `Signed-off-by:` trailer certifying you have the right to submit the change under the project's license (Developer Certificate of Origin)
An automatic squash of every prior commit on the branch
A trigger that forces CI to re-run on the pull request
